newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spain aims to join EMU starting group -- Aznar.
newsitem.headline: Spain aims to join EMU starting group -- Aznar.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, in an implicit rebuff to Germany, said his country was intent on qualifying for European Monetary Union (EMU) this year.

"Impertinent remarks without a factual basis are easily made. But afterward one must deny them and write letters of apology," he told the weekly Die Zeit in an interview to be published on Thursday to coincide with his visit to Bonn.

In a speech in Bonn, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato underlined Spain's determination not to be left out of the first wave of EMU members, saying qualification must be based purely on the economic criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty.
Germany, one of the loudest advocates of a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria, has said EMU is likely to start in January 1999 with a small core group of participants.

German state secretary of finance Juergen Stark, without naming particular countries, said on Tuesday some aspirants should forsake the political prestige of joining EMU at the outset and wait until their economies were well enough prepared.
His remark appeared to be aimed at countries like Italy or Spain that have not yet established a track record of exchange rate stability.
But Aznar said Spain must and would be among the founders of EMU. "The citizens are prepared for that and the government is committed to doing everything necessary to achieve it," he said.
He said Spain's commitment was more political than economic, as EMU was the way to the political integration of Europe.
Aznar said Spain would slash its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year, the target set by the Maastricht Treaty for participation in the single currency.
"Our budget for 1997 is the most stringent in 20 years. We will reach without problems the Maastricht goal of shrinking the deficit to three percent of GDP," he said.
Spain, Italy and Portugal are sometimes disparaged by northern European officials as the Club Med group, with high inflation, deficits and interest rates.
Germans fear the participation of the Club Med countries will soften the euro, making it vulnerable to inflation.

But now Germany itself, long a model of fiscal rectitude, is coming precariously close to missing the deficit goal. It has raised its forecast for this year's deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP, after 3.9 percent last year.
Aznar said Spain wants a strong euro as much as Germany and he also opposed a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
"I know no Club Med. I know only one treaty, which sets certain entry conditions for all. And I am working to see we fulfil these conditions," he said.
Rato sent a similar message to German industrialists in Bonn, telling them that people across Europe expected the EMU criteria in the Maastricht Treaty to be law.

He said Spain would have had to reform its economy and impose budget discipline even without Maastricht. "The decision made in 1998 (on who qualifies for EMU) has to be a decision based on the treaty. I have no doubt about that," he said.
